I have sat through maybe two hundred vendor pitches and I now ask the same four questions every time, in the same order, and I ask them out loud in the meeting rather than afterwards in an email. One. What exactly happens on day one if we say yes. Not the vision, the first two weeks. Two. Which of your existing clients is closest to us in size and in regulation, and can I call them. Three. What breaks first when the volume triples. Every system breaks somewhere and I would rather hear it from you than find it myself. And four. What would you need from my side that you have not asked for yet. That last one is the most useful question in the room, because it moves them from selling to planning, and you learn immediately whether they have actually done this before.

I sell to banks for a living, so let me tell you what happens on our side of the table. When a bank asks me for a reference client in the same regulatory environment, I know the deal is real and I take it to my head of delivery that evening. When a bank asks only about price in the first meeting, I quote high, because price is the only thing they have given me to compete on. And when somebody asks what breaks first at three times the volume, I will be honest with you, half of my competitors cannot answer that question at all. So the questions do not just get you information. They tell me who I am dealing with, and they change what I bring to the second meeting.

There is a pattern in failed technology procurement that shows up again and again in the reviews afterwards, and it is almost never about the technology. The decision goes wrong at the point where the buying side accepts a claim without turning it into a condition. A supplier says integration typically takes twelve weeks. Typically. Nobody asks what would make it twenty, and twenty is what it becomes. A supplier says the platform scales. Nobody asks to what, or what happens at the point where it stops. The fix is not scepticism and it is not more meetings. It is one habit, which is to turn every claim on the page into a sentence beginning with if. If the integration runs past sixteen weeks, then what. If the regulator changes the reporting rule in March, then what. A claim you cannot turn into an if is usually a claim the supplier has not tested either.
